newsitem.title: USA: Dow hits 3rd record in week; bonds, dollar rally.
newsitem.headline: Dow hits 3rd record in week; bonds, dollar rally.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average rose to a record for the third time this week as interest rates fell Thursday after a government report pointed to tame inflation.
The dollar surged. Oil prices fell.
The Dow index jumped 76.19 points to 6,625.67, beating the record of 6,600.66, set on Tuesday. It briefly climbed more than 100 points in late afternoon before backtracking on profit-taking.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,610 to 931 on heavy volume of 554 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Stocks got a boost from the government's December Producer Price Index (PPI), which confirmed that inflation remained in check at the wholesale level.

The report sparked a sharp rally in the bond market, lifting the benchmark 30-year Treasury more than a full point and lowering its yield 6.75 percent from 6.84 percent on Wednesday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

Overall, wholesale prices rose 0.5 percent in December, the department reported. While the increase was more than economists had generally forecast, most of the rise was attributable to higher energy prices.
The so-called "core" rate, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose a scant 0.1 percent, which was in line with analysts' forecasts.
With pressure on interest rates waning, investors held to a path they have repeatedly taken recently and seized the opportunity to buy after Wednesday's 51-point drop in the Dow.
"The conventional wisdom is still to buy on every dip," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co.
The market kept with another recent trend, Metz noted, because most of the buying was focused on large stocks.
"In general, the money is coming in through intermediaries like mutual fund managers and they are still opting to buy the big names," he said.
The flood of cash finding its way to mutual funds has aided the market's ascent.

"We're in the midst of the deployment of funds that takes place at the beginning of the year," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "That liquidity is still a powerful driver for this market."

So powerful, analysts said, that investors were apparently able to overcome the caution that generally creeps in ahead of the closely watched monthly employment report, due out on Friday and widely considered more important than the PPI.

"I've got to say this rally is rather impressive ahead of what is supposed to be an important number," Metz said, adding that among indicators on the economy and inflation, he ranked the employment report "No. 1."
The dollar rose to 116.37 Japanese yen from 115.72 late Wednesday and to 1.5775 German marks from 1.5749. The U.S. currency rose to 1.3695 Swiss francs from 1.3645.
At the New York Mecantile Exchange, oil prices slid amid rampant rumours that gasoline cargoes from Europe due to arrive this month in New York Harbour, a key hub.

February unleaded gasoline closed 1.71 cents a gallon lower at 70.48 cents.The steep decline sent February heating oil down 0.38 cent a gallon to end at 73.05 cents and February crude down 25 cents to finish at $26.37 a barrel.
Overseas, Tokyo's Nikkei average of 225 leading shares fell 606.51 points to 18,073.87 and London's FTSE 100 index fell 0.5 point to 4,087.0.
